en: *ie2>* Dinakarī:
The meaning is "when power (*śakti*) has been established by the reasoning previously stated. Regarding the phrase "conducive to burning" (*dāhānukūla*): here...

Furthermore, "conformity" (anukūlatva) is common to both [the cause] and that which delimits the causal status; therefore, there is no deficiency even if power (*śakti*) serves as the delimiter of causal status. The word "is destroyed" (*nāśyate*) is to be construed with "is postulated" (*kalpyate*).
Thus, with respect to that which is delimited by the property of being a power residing in fire (*vahni*), [the following applies].

The point is that by accepting the jewel as the destroyer [of the power], there is no burning precisely because the power is absent during the state when the jewel and other such things are present. Now, an objection: if the jewel and so forth are the destroyers of the power, then when the jewel is either qualified by the presence of an excitant (*uttejaka*) or has been removed, burning would not occur. To this [the author replies]:
He says: "by means of the excitant" (*utejakena*). [Objection: If the jewel and so forth are removed, burning would not occur;
therefore he says: "by means of the excitant. In the phrase "and by the removal of the jewel and so forth," the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "or" (*vā*).
Nor is it the case that, because one might postulate the absence of the jewel (*maṇyabhāva*) as the cause for burning, [burning does not occur] at the time of the presence of the jewel.

It should rather be stated that "the burner" [is the cause], because it is cumbersome to postulate the independent causality of the absence of a jewel (*maṇyabhāva*) as a property; for it is more appropriate to postulate the causality of fire by virtue of its possessing a distinct power (*śakti*). This is the underlying intention. Now, if this were so...
If it is argued that even if power (*śakti*) is established, its existence as something distinct [from the categories] is not proven, we say no;

for it is not included among the aforementioned categories. To explain: power is certainly not of the nature of substance (*dravya*), because it resides in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. For this very reason, it is neither of the nature of quality nor of the nature of action (*karman*).

Nor is it of the nature of any one of the [categories] beginning with generality (*sāmānya*), because it is perishable while being subject to origination. Thus, having established that power (*śakti*) is a distinct entity, he establishes that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is also a distinct category by means of the passage beginning with "evam" (thus).
Regarding the word "distinct" (*atirikta*): the meaning is that it is distinct from the seven categories already established.

The reason—"because, while not being included within the six categories (ṣaḍpadārtha), it is not included within non-existence (abhāva)"—must be supplied [to the argument]. Therein, he dispels the charge of the unestablished nature of the qualification (*satyanta-asiddhi*) with the words "for that... (*taddhi*). That is similarity (*sādṛśya*);
"hi" indicates the reason. "Even in the case of a universal" (*sāmānye'pi*) means: provided that it subsists in both the universal and its opposite.
The meaning is "because it exists as a universal. Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to being a universal (*sāmānyatva*).
Because of the qualification "provided it is negative" (*vyatirekitve sati*), there is no deviation with respect to knowability (*prameyatva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since the probandum exists even in the probans—which consists of being one of the six categories beginning with substance (*dravya*)—there is no deviation with respect to being an existent (*bhāvatva*).

Regarding the term "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*): as for the phrase "for example," the meaning is that if similarity were included within [the categories of] substance (*dravya*) and so forth, then since substance and the like do not subsist in universals (*sāmānya*), there would be no such uncontradicted cognition as "just as cowness is eternal, so too is horseness."

Anticipating the objection that [non-existence] might be included within [existence], he refutes it with the words "nor also" (*nāpi*). Although the consideration of inclusion within existence is impossible in the view of the Prābhākara—who does not admit a non-existent entity as something distinct—nevertheless, this has been refuted while provisionally accepting the opponent's position; such is the intention. "As existence" (*satvena*) means as a positive entity (*bhāvatvena*).

"Because it is being perceived" means because it is being cognized. He refutes the *śakti* (potency) established by the Prābhākara in order to prevent the occurrence of burning from fire when a gem is present—stating "in the absence of the gem, etc. [He does so] because of the postulation of a separate potency (*atirikta-śakti*).

The point is that, rather than postulating the aforementioned relationship between the destroyed and the destroyer, it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to postulate that the cause for [the production of] burning as delimited by the property of being-burning (dāhatva-avacchinna) is simply the state of being fire qualified by the absence of a jewel (maṇyabhāva-viśiṣṭa-vahni-tva). The phrase "burning and so forth" includes fire by means of the word "and so forth" (ādi-pada).
The meaning is that even from fire accompanied by a jewel (*maṇi*), burning does not arise;
thus, because of the presence of the obstacle consisting of the form of the jewel, there is no burning. [Objection:
But then, at some time or other, burning would result from fire qualified by the absence of the jewel. Dinakarī.
Because it is precisely the existence of a cause as delimited by the delimitor of causal status (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) that determines the production of an effect, and because—
regarding whether "fire qualified by the absence of a jewel" or "the absence of a jewel qualified by fire" is the delimitor of causal status—

there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) for the status of qualifier and qualified, which would result in the undesirable consequence of two cumbersome cause-and-effect relations. Therefore...

He says: "due to the absence of the jewel, etc. And thus, obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatva*) does not consist in the disruption of a property conducive to the effect, because that would entail the consequence that the cognition of a sublation (*bādhajñāna*) lacks the status of being an obstructor of inference. Rather, [it consists in]...

The meaning is that [the definition] consists in being the counter-positive of an absence that has become a cause; and this is only possible if the absence of the jewel (maṇi) is the cause, but not if there exists a separate potency (śakti). Now, if the state of being an obstructor (pratibandhakatva) is intended here, then [the definition applies] to that which is the counter-positive of an absence whose nature is the fire that has become a cause, as stated in the Dinakarī.

If it is argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of other entities (*anyabhāva*) and in the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*) which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of its own prior non-existence (*svaprāgabhāva*), we say no. [The definition refers to] being the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)— which is distinct from a positive entity (*bhāvabhina*) and serves as the locus (*āśraya*) of a causality (*kāraṇatā*) delimited by a relation other than identity (*tādātmya*).

This is because [the self] is intended [as the locus], and because it would follow that the self is an obstacle to the perception of its own absolute non-existence due to the adoption of a specific causal status;
this is refuted, since the object is the cause of perception only through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). Now, [an objection]:

Since both the absence of the jewel (*maṇi*) and its non-existence (*abhāva*) are causes [of burning], it is more appropriate that a single, distinct power (*śakti*) alone be the cause, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*); therefore, he says: "By this very [means]. This means: by the mere postulation of the absence of the jewel and so forth as the cause with respect to burning and the like. [This is sufficient for] consistency (*sāmajasye*).

Regarding the prevention of burning when there is contact with a jewel, since there is no evidence for the prior absence (prāgabhāva) [of the power], he says "destruction" (*dhvaṃsa*). This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the destruction of the counter-positive and the destruction of the power, as well as the removal of the power and the removal of the jewel.
It should also be understood that the conceptualization of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) may likewise apply. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of an excitant" (*utejakābhāve*):

thus, it is not the jewel alone that is the obstructer (*pratibandhaka*), but rather the jewel as qualified by the absence of an excitant; and this [qualified] absence persists even at the time when an excitant is present.

The meaning is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Now, if it is argued that in cases such as those involving a jewel (*maṇi*) and so forth, the counter-inflamer (*pratyuttejaka*) itself should be the cause [of burning], we say no; for that [counter-inflamer] lacks a commonality (*ananugatatva*), whereas the absence of the jewel qualified by the aggregate of its absences (*tadabhāvakūṭaviśiṣṭamaṇyabhāva*) possesses a commonality. Here, this should be understood: [the cause is] by way of the relation of "qualifier-ness" belonging to an absence (*abhāvīyaviśeṣaṇatā-sambandha*).
With respect to that which is delimited by the state of being burning (*dāhatva*),

there is a specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) consisting in the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the respective absences of excitants (*uttejaka*), whose counterpositiveness is delimited by either the objective-qualifierhood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka-viśeṣaṇatā*) or the subjective-qualifierhood (*vidheyatāvacchedaka-viśeṣaṇatā*). That which is delimited by such [co-occurrence]...

The probans (hetu) is the absence of the absence of a jewel and so forth, where the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of that absence is delimited by either the relation of being a qualifier of the locus (ādeśika-viśeṣaṇatā) or the relation of being the intended object (uddeśyatā); this absence [of the absence] stands in the relation of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatā-saṃbandha).
By this, even in that which is conjoined with it, there is the absence of a jewel whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga-saṃbandha).

Thus, the objection that "the production of burning would follow from [fire's] existence" is refuted. Now, it may be argued that inference alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding potency (*śakti*).

For instance: fire is the inherent locus (*samavāyin*) of a certain invisible property (*adṛṣṭa-dharma*) conducive to burning, because it produces burning, just like the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the self. [This argument fails] by taking into account the fire in a binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*), or by taking into account the unmanifest color (*anudbhūta-rūpa*) residing in the fire within a frying pan.

Or, in order to avoid proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanavāraṇa*), the term "conducive to burning" (*dāhānukūla*) is included in the probandum (*sādhya*). To exclude [the probandum] by taking as the cause the conjunction of the triad (*tryaṇuka*) with fuel, or the conjunction of the self possessing unseen merit (*adṛṣṭavat-ātman*) with it, the term "inherent" (*ādhiṣṭhate*) is used. To exclude [the probandum] by taking the hot touch residing in fire as the cause, the term "transcendental" (*atīndriya*) is used.
If it is argued that this is not so, we say no; for this inference is not probative (*aprayojaka*) due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*) against the contrary case (*vipakṣa*).
Some, however, [hold that] regarding fire, the causal efficiency (*kāraṇatā*) of the contact between grass and blowing, etc., exists in the form of "grass-blowing-contact-ness," etc.

Due to the impossibility [of such a relation] because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), an additional power (*atirikta-śakti*) is established. Furthermore, there is no single property that delimits the state of being produced (*janya-tāvacchedaka*) for the relation between grass and blowing, the fire-drill and friction, or the jewel and its rays.

It should not be argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because one must postulate three distinct universals (vaijātya) residing in the subsistence of the fire-possessing entity (vahnimad-vṛtti);
for it is simpler to assume that those various relations possess a single power (śakti), rather than postulating three universals as the delimiters of being produced by them (tajjanyatāvacchedaka).
They say that the postulation of [the universal] *kāraṇatva* (causality) itself is more reasonable because of its parsimony;

but that is not so, because we accept only a single genus (*jāti*) as being common to all those various relations. Nor should it be argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence that a genus existing in a perceptible locus would itself have to be perceptible, for [this is avoided] by means of a specific defect (*doṣaviśeṣa*).

This is because one assumes that the capacity [of the cause] is otherwise unfit for that effect. Nor is there any confusion [of categories] with respect to "pushing-ness" (*nodanatva*) and so forth, since such confusion is not a fault and because causality is possible through the property of being "one of several" (*anyatamatva*).
Furthermore, regarding the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified among the individual differences (*bheda*) that constitute "being one of several,"...

It should not be argued that there is a multiplicity of causal powers (*kāraṇatā*) due to the difference in the delimiters of those powers (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), because of the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*); for it is possible to establish the unity of the causal power by treating as one the various distinct delimiters that are co-extensive (*samaniyata*). Nor can it be said that this is impossible because the differences themselves cannot serve as delimiters in their own right.

One must state that the delimiting nature (*avacchedakatva*) [of the respective causes] is determined by such factors as: the difference characterized by the conjunction of blowing on grass, the difference characterized by the contact of rubbing the fire-drills, and the difference delimited by the relation between the jewel and its rays.

And thus, due to the difference in the delimiters of the delimiting nature (*avacchedakatāvacchedaka-bheda*), there is a difference in the delimiting natures themselves; and due to that difference, [there is a difference in the resulting effects].

It must be stated that there is a distinction in causal efficacy (*kāraṇatā*), whether this causal efficacy consists in the nature of the thing itself (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) or is something distinct; thus says Dinakara.
"Even when there is a difference in the delimitors (*avacchedaka*), there is non-difference [of the effect]," as is explained in detail elsewhere. Others,

however, say that since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) for establishing a single potency, one cannot establish a potency by taking the air-contact (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) occurring at the time of contact with grass and so forth as the cause on the grounds that they possess a single potency.

He also refutes the suspicion that similarity (*sādṛśya*) might be a distinct category of entity by stating, "even similarity," and "provided it is different from that. This [qualification] is intended to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to that which defines similarity. When there is an intention to specify the relation as *anuyogitā* (the property of being the locus of comparison),...
But it must certainly be granted that [the definition] consists in possessing many properties residing in that [subject].

The meaning is: possessing those numerous properties which exist there [in the subject] by way of being unique (asādhāraṇya). Dinakari: Now, this [is like saying]: "The sky is like the sky; the ocean is comparable to the ocean; the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa..."

If it is argued that [the definition] is under-extensive (avyāpta) in cases such as "like Rāma and Rāvaṇa," we say no; for in those instances, what is intended to be expressed is merely a property residing in them, or else, because difference exists there through the intention to express a distinction between the ages (yuga-bheda). Therefore, when a distinction between the ages is intended, the figure of speech here is Simile (upamā-alaṃkāra); otherwise, it is the figure of Non-comparison (ananvaya-alaṃkāra).

Thus it has been stated by the Alaṃkārikas. Furthermore, the attribute that constitutes similarity may sometimes be of the nature of a genus (*jāti*), as in "the cloth is similar to the jar," and so forth; or it may be of the nature of an adventitious quality (*upādhi*), as in "just as cowness is eternal, so too is horseness," or as in "the face is like the moon," where the attribute is such as "producing delight," and so on.

"Because it would involve the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate [similarity] as something distinct. The *Dinakarī* states: "The moderns (*navya*), however, maintain that similarity is indeed a distinct category.

Nor should it be argued that if it were distinct, it would contradict the classification of categories (*padārtha-vibhāga*); for that [classification] is intended merely to describe all categories whatsoever that are useful for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), whether directly or indirectly. The *Dinakarī* states: [End of section].

Likewise, they say that if its nature were conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, then since conjunction is resident in both terms—as in the case of the conjunction between a jujube fruit and a bowl—the usage "the bowl in the jujube fruit" would occur just as one says "the jujube fruit in the bowl.
They further maintain that the same would apply to the nature of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*). [Now follows] the definition of similarity (*sādṛśya*).

He applies [this] to the object of illustration with the words "yathā" (as for example). The word "iti" indicates the completion of the commentary on the verse. || 2 || Since the word *kṣiti*, which ends in the suffix *ktin* prescribed by the rule "striyāṃ ktin," denotes destruction (*kṣaya*), [the following applies].
He states the meaning relevant to the present context regarding the word *kṣitipa*: "the earth is the *pṛthivī*.
Regarding the word *āpa*, he says "the waters are the *jalāni*" because, in Pāṇini’s sūtra "aptṛn tṛca," etc., the term refers to the word-form itself.
Furthermore, since *pratāpa* (valor) is also denoted by the word *tejas* (splendor), [he uses it] in the present context...

He shows the referent of the term *tejas* (fire/heat) with the words "fire, etc. (*tejo vahnir iti*). The meaning is "fire and so forth. Since a particular deity is also denoted by the word *marut*, he states the meaning relevant to the present context: "Marut is wind" (*marud vāyur iti*).
Because the word *vyoman* is used in the Veda to denote Brahman, he says: "vyoma means ākāśa.

Because the word *kāla* conveys meanings such as the Ender (Antaka) and so forth, he says: "kāla means time (*samaya*). [Regarding] the word *dik*, which is derived from the verbal root *diś* in the sense of "bestowing" (*atisarjana*).
Because it has the sense of "giving," he states the meaning relevant to the present context: "the directions and so forth.
Since the word *dehin* (embodied) denotes an object qualified by a body, and because the limbs of the body are thereby brought to mind, he says:
"the embodied one is the self (*ātman*). Now, since the Lord is not included among the embodied beings, how can He be the "melted" (*drava*)?

If it is objected [that this is not so], we say no; for the elders maintain that the Lord has a body according to the analogy of possession by a spirit (*bhūtāveśanyāya*). Others hold that he possesses a body due to the influence of the perceptions of transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*).

Precisely because of this lack of consensus, he states "the Self" (*ātman*). There are only five substances: earth, water, fire, air, and the Self, since space and the other elements are included within the very nature of the Lord.

The moderns say that the mind (manas) is included among the non-inherent substances; in order to refute their view, he states the meaning by supplying the word indicating the number: "These are the nine substances.
First, the establishment of space (vyoman) is through its being the substratum of sound. Nor is it the case that the Lord alone is the substratum of sound.

Since there is no reason for singling out one [individual] over another (*vinigamanāviraha*), it would have to be accepted that each individual soul (*jīva*) [possesses the quality]. Furthermore, if the souls were the substrata, there would be the cognition "I am the possessor of sound" (*śabdavān aham*).
(Dinakarī)

There is no contradiction with perception, because one postulates only that which is unobservable and unfit for perception. As for time and space, they [are established] from such uniform cognitions as "the jar is at this time" and "the cloth is in the eastern direction. And as for the mind, since it is not composed of the elements...

The intention is that there would be no basis for selection (*vinigamanāviraha*) if one were to take the atoms of earth and so forth; this will become clearer further on. Regarding the term "substances" (*dravyāṇi*) in the root text: the word *dravya* signifies an object qualified by the universal (*jāti*) of substantiality (*dravyatva*), and not...

The term [“substance”] has as its meaning that which is qualified by being the locus of qualities, because of the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). As for the question “What is the proof for [the existence of] ‘pearls’ (*muktāvalī*)?”—the word *kiṃ* is used in the sense of an inquiry. Now, one might object: “Surely the uniform cognition (anugata-pratīti) ‘this is a substance, this is a substance’ itself will serve as the proof for the universal (*jāti*”). To this he says: “Not so. In that context—that is, regarding the universal of substanceness (*dravyatva-jāti*).

Regarding "ghṛta" (clarified butter) and so forth: according to the Dinakarī, since common people lack the cognition of "substance-ness" (dravyatva) with respect to clarified butter and similar things, [the definition would fail to apply].
The sense is that the establishment of the genus *dravyatva* (substanceness), which is common to all substances, will not be possible.

Regarding the term "kārya" (effect): *kāryatva* (the state of being an effect) consists in being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Nor is there the fault of over-extension to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), because [the definition] is qualified by the property of existence (*satva*). And in this context, the inherence (*samavāya*) of the effect [is intended].

Proximity [is the relation], namely the identity (tādātmya) of the cause; for there is a rule that wherever the effect exists by way of inherence (samavāya), there the substance exists by way of identity. Now, one might object: there is no evidence for the causal status of "substance-ness" as the cause, with respect to the effect delimited by "being a product" (janyasattva-rūpa-kāryatva) through the relation of identity. Nor [is it sufficient to say] "in the case of blue..."

It must be stated that, in order to exclude blue lotuses [from being causes], causality is likewise necessary; for that exclusion is already achieved by blue being the cause of blue [color] through the relation of "inherence in a substance inherent in its own locus" (svāśrayasamavetadravyatvasambandha),
whereas taking "effectness" as the delimiting property of effectness would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

Because there would be a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) due to the inclusion of "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) and so forth through the relation of temporal succession (*kālikasaṃbandha*), he says: "of conjunction" (*saṃyogasya*).

And here, qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth are excluded from being effects of substance because they do not reside in all substances; likewise, the triad beginning with number (*saṃkhyā*), which resides in all substances, is excluded because it resides in [eternal] entities such as space (*ākāśa*) due to its eternity. Nor is [substance-ness] a cause for that which is delimited by the universal "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*).

It should not be argued that there is a lack of evidence for [the self] being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because it is necessary for each specific individual (*tattadvyakti*) to be an inherent cause with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*) inhering in that individual, and thus its production in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth would be impossible; for there is a rule that a universal residing in every effect must necessarily be the delimiting factor of the state of being an effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).

Because such causality is necessary. He states "of disjunction" (vibhāgasya) in a manner common to the views of those who accept eternal conjunction. "From the establishment of substantiality" (dravyatvasiddheḥ) means from the establishment of the genus *dravyatva*. In some places, the reading is exactly as it stands. Here...

Although it is possible for [the probans] to be otherwise established as a quality (*guṇa*), the point is that an inference has as its object a property connected through a causal chain only when there is a sublation of a property directly connected [to the subject]. This is also an illustration: because another substance does not arise within a substance, [the probans] exists in a substance by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

The Dinakarī states: "Obstructiveness must be postulated. Thus, the universal *dravyatva* (substance-ness) is established as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of obstructiveness. However, the delimiting factor of the state of being obstructed (*pratibadhyatā*) is simply the property of being an element (*bhūtatva*) that resides exclusively in the four [elements] beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*), because it excludes eternal substances.

If, however, *bhūtatva* (the state of being an element) were the delimiting factor of the obstructive capacity (*pratibandhakatāvacchedakatva*), then there would be an absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) by taking *mūrtatva* (corporeality) to be such a factor; whereas the fact that *dravyatva* (substantiality) is the delimiting factor of the obstructive capacity is established by the means of knowledge that apprehends the locus (*dharmigrāhakamāna*). Nor is there a lack of evidence for its subsistence in [entities] such as space (*gagana*).

This must be said: because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of having an equal number of individual instances (*tulyavyaktikatva*) by virtue of being an element (*bhūtatva*), and due to the absence of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*), one would have to admit that [the universal *dravyatva*] resides in five things, such as space (*gagana*) and so forth. Nor can it be argued that, in order to avoid this equality of instances by virtue of being an element, one should instead postulate that [the universal *dravyatva*] resides in the mind (*manas*) alone.
It should not be argued that there is complexity (gaurava) in postulating [the quality of] residing in space and so forth, because even when such residence is postulated,
the quality of residing in the mind must necessarily be admitted in order to avoid the fault of overlap (sāṃkarya) with corporeality (mūrtatva).
For if that were the case, then [the definition of] substancehood (dravyatva) would [overlap] with the universal (jāti) of corporeality.

"Because it would follow that [darkness] has the same nature as a manifest individual. Now, with the intention that the statement "there are nine substances" is incorrect because darkness—the tenth substance—actually exists, the Mīmāṃsaka raises an objection: "But surely... and so on.
Indeed.

Anticipating the objection that darkness was not mentioned because there is a lack of evidence for its existence, [the author] states the perceptual means of knowledge (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*) that establishes darkness: "taddhi" (for that). The meaning is "for darkness indeed."

By "perceptually" means by the sense-organ of sight. Now, one might object: even if darkness is established [as an object], what is the proof for its being a substance? Anticipating this doubt, he states the means of knowledge through inference—namely, "of that. This refers to darkness.
The word "and" (ca) connects with the term "substance-hood. Thus, darkness is a substance.

It has been indicated that the inference "because it possesses color" (*rūpavattvāt*) is the proof for the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of darkness. This is an elliptical indication; it should also be understood as "because it is the locus of priority and so forth" (*paratvādyāśrayatvāt*), since there is the cognition: "This darkness is further, this [other] is nearer. Now, an objection: there is no evidence for color in darkness, is there not? No.

Nor should it be said that its existence is established through the cognition "this is blue darkness," because such a cognition is erroneous; therefore, he states another reason: "because it possesses action" (*karmavatvāt*). And by "possessing action," what is intended is the relation of inherence (*samavāya*); for otherwise, every produced thing would [be considered dark] by virtue of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).

Even though it possesses action, there is no deviation [from the definition]; nor is there a lack of proof regarding its essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), because its possession of action is established by the cognition "the shadow moves. He refutes the inclusion of darkness (*tamas*) within the already established substances by means of the words beginning with "that" (*taddhi*), etc., and [the word] "smell," etc.

If it were stated that "the absence of odor" is the reason [for the inference], there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a jar, because one could take as the probans the absence whose counter-positive is the odor residing in a cloth; therefore, "emptiness" (*śūnyatva*) is specified. Furthermore, the reason must be non-co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*), even when its counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

It should be understood [as follows]: by this, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a jar that exists at a time other than its production, nor in a jar that lacks the absence of fragrance as delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Regarding "blue color" (*nīlarūpa*): it is by means of a single, uniform blue color as the probans (*hetu*).

Since the distinction of the eightfold division beginning with water is established, non-concomitant properties such as the absence of viscidity have not been presented as the reasons; by the phrase "water and so forth," substances such as fire and the rest are included. And thus, among the nine [substances]...

The point is that, since it is impossible for darkness to be included within [the other] substances, its status as an additional substance is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). As it has been said: "Darkness is indeed mobile, blue, and possesses the distinctions of priority and posteriority; because of its dissimilarity to the [other] well-known substances, it deserves to be distinguished from the nine [substances]. Now, if darkness is a substance...

There would be no apprehension by the visual faculty independent of light, because the visual faculty dependent on light is the cause for the apprehension of substances; therefore, he says: "And in the perception of that. This means: "and in the perception of darkness. [The meaning is: that which is delimited by being a visual perception of a substance distinct from darkness.

The meaning is that lightness is determined to be the cause [of visual perception] by way of the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with respect to light itself. Regarding the phrase "by the necessary absence of light":
this means by the absence of that which is delimited by the nature of light (*tejas*), which possesses excellence of magnitude, manifested color, and non-overpowering color.
"But why should light not simply be the absence of darkness?"—this objection from the *Dinakari* is not correct;

for it is necessary [to state] that [otherwise] the cognition of hot touch and luminous color would be unaccounted for. "In the case of its being accounted for" means: in the case of the accountability of the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding darkness. Now, if darkness were the absence of light...

"How can there be the cognition of possessing form, given that in the absence [of matter] there is an absence of form? To this he says: "Possessing form. Now, even if the cognition of possessing form is erroneous, fluidity will still be established by the reason of possessing action, as proven by the cognition "it moves. To this [he replies]: [The text continues: ...because it is not perceived in the absence of matter. Therefore, he says: "Possessing form. Now, one might object: even if the cognition of possessing form is an error, fluidity will nonetheless be established by the reason of possessing action, which is proven by the cognition "it moves. To this...

He says: "The perception of possessing action [is also [erroneous]). The meaning is that the perception of possessing action in a substance is not due to any other external condition (*upādhi*). Now, one accepts the erroneous nature of a perception only in cases where a sublation (*bādhajñāna*) occurs at a later time; and in the present case, there is the cognition: "Darkness does not move."
To the objection that the cognition [of darkness] cannot be erroneous because there is no subsequent sublation (*bādhajñāna*), he states another refutation:
"Of darkness... By the phrase "parts, etc.," the inclusion of origination and destruction is intended. As for the claim that darkness is a superimposed blue form...

This is the view of Kandali-kāra. [Dinakari]: That is not correct; for it would follow that even the cognition "here is great darkness" would be an error, and because there is the perception that "darkness is blue, but not blueness.
Now, even if darkness is not a distinct entity, gold is a distinct substance.
Since the contradiction regarding the non-existence of *sattva* remains exactly as it was, he says: "of gold.

[The phrase] "will be stated" implies that this will occur on the occasion of defining *tejas* (fire/light). || 3 || [The phrase] "explicitly" refers to: "Color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, and posteriority..."

In the *Vibhāga-sūtra*, seventeen qualities are explicitly mentioned by name: "Intellects, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and efforts are the qualities. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the sūtra, the qualities of gravity, fluidity, viscidity, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), merit and demerit (*dharmādharma*), and sound are included. And these—

All [qualities] taken together are here conventionally designated as the four hundred and thirty. [Objection: But why is "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) not [the defining characteristic] of the four hundred and thirty? Nor is it a specific genus (*jāti*), because there is no evidence for that. To this he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). This means "among the qualities. [This will be explained] further on.

"At the occasion of defining the qualities (guṇa), it will be stated. The meaning is that the inference—"The causality residing in that which is distinct from substance (dravya) and action (karman) and possesses generality (sāmānya) must be delimited by some property (dharma), because it is causality"—is the proof for the genus "quality-ness" (guṇatva). This truth will become clear in that very place.
"Established by perception" means that it is cognized by a cognition conforming to the form of motion.

"By way of being additional" means by means of the class-characteristics that differentiate actions, such as *bhramaṇatva* (rotationality) and so forth. [In the] root-text, "from motion (*gamanāt*) alone":

now, if it is argued that since even throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest are included within motion, and since [the definition] is obtained from "motion alone," the classification by means of *utkṣepaṇatva* and so forth is redundant;
for indeed, in throwing upwards and the like...

If it is argued that "the state of being in motion" is not based on direct perception, because there arises the cognition that a clod of earth thrown upwards or downwards "goes upwards" or "goes downwards," we say no; for a Sage (muni), who possesses independent will, is not subject to the constraints of injunctions or prohibitions. 6–7. As for the definition of that [motion]: [The text continues: "But its characteristic is... [Note: The provided fragment ends here.]
The purpose [of this definition] is the establishment of the distinction of "generality" from others, or the establishment of its conventional usage;

that is, generality is distinct from others—such as substance and so forth—or it is the object of the conventional usage "this is a generality," because, while being eternal, it inheres in many things. Whatever is not thus, is not thus.
As in the case of "substance" (*dravya*). This should be inferred for other definitions as well. Multiplicity (*anekatva*) is the state of being different from unity (*ekabhinnatva*).
The qualifying portion [of the definition] was stated to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such things as the color of a water-atom (*jalaparamāṇu-rūpa*).
He states the purpose of the *samavāya* (inherence) that constitutes the property of "inhering" (*samavetatva*) as follows: "the state of existing in multiple [substances] while being eternal.
Nor should it be argued that there is thus over-extension to eternal conjunction (*nityasaṃyoga*), for that has already been refuted.

If it is asked, "Why is there no [inclusion of] *nirāsa* (exclusion)?"— the answer is no; because in the system that accepts eternal conjunction (*nityasaṃyoga*), there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) if one were to include "being produced" (*janyatva*) within the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka-koṭi*) of the effectness residing in conjunction, which is not itself delimited by the causalness residing in substance.

Since the property of being a conjunction (*saṃyogatva*) resides in eternal [entities], it cannot be the delimiting factor for being an effect; furthermore, by the same reasoning, it would follow that eternal disjunction (*nityavibhāga*) must also be established. Anticipating the objection that [conjunction] lacks the property of inhering in more than one [substance], he provides the answer by stating that it is "merely a single individual" (*ekavyaktimātra*), thereby indicating that it is not the subject of the definition (*alakṣya*).

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) consisting in the non-difference of the individual. The intended meaning is that there is an absence of a continuous cognition (*anugatadhi*) which would postulate a universal (*jāti*). Now, it might be argued that the non-difference of the individual is itself unestablished as a subverter of the universal, given that [the individual] is devoid of a commonality while being distinct from a particular (*viśeṣa*).

Since the definition of a universal (*jāti*) consists in its inherence in many [substances], he cites the consensus of authorities by stating, "And thus it has been said. The remainder of the sentence is: "by the teacher Udayana in the *Dravyakiraṇāvalī*. This is because a single property that resides in many is universally established as a universal (*sāmānya*), whereas in a single individual instance...

The meaning is that a universal (*jāti*) is not admitted [in such cases]. The absence of difference between individuals—that is, having only a single individual—is the subverting argument against [treating] "space-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and the like as universals. Dinakarī: Equality consists in subsisting in the same number of individuals, as in the case of the difference between universals such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "jar-ness" (*kalaśatva*). In reality, however...
The meaning is as follows: "equality" means being co-extensive with a genus different from one's own;

and it should be understood that this [equality] is indeed a sublater of [the existence of] a genus. Furthermore, "confusion" (*saṃkara*) consists in the simultaneous occurrence in a single locus of two properties that are each co-locative with the absolute non-existence of the other.

There is an objection to the status of *bhūtatva* (elementality) and the like as universals (*jāti*). This is because *mūrtatva* (corporeality), which exists in the mind (*manas*) while excluding *bhūtatva*, and *bhūtatva*, which exists in space (*gagana*) while excluding *mūrtatva*, both coexist in the four [substances] beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*). Now, one might ask: what is the role of this "intermixture" (*sāṃkarya*) in invalidating the status of a universal?

If it is argued that this is a definition, [it is not so], because [the property] is delimited by the nature of being a specific universal (jātiviśeṣa) qualified by the universal-ness (jātitva), through the dual relation of co-referentiality with itself and co-referentiality with its own absence.

The moderns [the Naiyāyikas] maintain that there is no proof for such a rule, and thus the confusion of classes (*sāṃkarya*) does not constitute a sublation of their status as universals (*jāti*); however, infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would indeed apply if a universal were itself possessed of a universal. Although...

Even if one accepts a single distinctness (*vaijātya*) across all universals (*jāti*), there is no further distinctness within that distinctness itself, because it resides in a single individual; nevertheless, one must understand that there is a single distinctness across all universals, and yet another distinctness among that distinctness and the universals that are its substrata, and so on ad infinitum— thus an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is to be recognized.

The loss of form (*rūpahāni*) consists in the contradiction of the definition of a *viśeṣa* (ultimate particular) as being devoid of a commonality (*niḥsāmānya*). Alternatively, it is the loss of the form’s own inherent capacity to differentiate (*svato vyāvartakatva*). In that case, if a genus (*jāti*) were admitted, the capacity to differentiate would have to be attributed to that genus alone; for that which is the substratum of a generality can only be differentiated by means of that generality itself.

Because there is a rule that [a property] must be a differentiator; nor is it possible for particulars to establish difference by means of a universal form, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For if such a rule were not accepted, then the singularities residing in atoms would [have to be established] merely as their respective individual instances (*tattadvyaktitvena*).

However, the superior view is that the particular (*viśeṣa*) would be rendered useless because it could be established by the differentiation between atoms themselves. [In this context,] "non-connection" refers to the absence of any connection, whether as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) or as a correlate (*anuyogitā*). (Dinakari)

"Absence of inherence [is a genus] because both inherence and absence possess the property of being a genus. And "with respect to that" means "with respect to existence (*sattā*). Furthermore, the genus existence is established precisely by the uniform cognitions such as "the substance exists," "the quality exists," and so forth. Regarding this, the moderns (*navya*) say:

Existence (*bhāvatva*) alone is the object of the cognition "existent" (*san-niti-pratīti*). For this very reason, even in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, there is the linguistic usage "existent," but there is no separate universal called "existence" (*satā*) residing in the triad beginning with substance (*dravya*).
Therefore, the Vaiśeṣika classification of universals as twofold—higher (*para*) and lower (*apara*)—with the higher being "existence" (*satā*), [is rejected].

They say that [the existence of "Being"] is unacceptable because it lacks logical justification; but that is not correct, because the genus *sat* (Being) is established as the delimitor of the causal capacity for destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Wherever there is the arising of destruction by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), there alone is there Being by way of the relation of identity (*tādātmya*).

[This is] because of the causal relation based on the proximity of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*), since [the effect] is absent while the antecedent absence exists; for the relation that delimits the state of being an effect is the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) distinct from the counter-correlativity residing in the antecedent absence. In reality, however, [the relation is] by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

The existence universal (*sattājāti*) is established as the delimiting factor of the effect-ness (*janyatāvacchedaka*) because substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is the cause with respect to [the production of] that which is delimited by existence through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). However, it is not the case that there is a lack of evidence for such a causal relationship;
for even in the case of blue and so forth, [blue-ness and the like] exist in blue and so forth through the relation of inherence in what is inherent in itself (*svāśrayasamavetatva*).
Because of its existence therein, [the causal relation] is like that of the sun;
for the sake of precluding the production of a blue lotus, such a causal relationship is necessary. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that such an undesirable consequence does not arise because blue and other qualities function as causes by way of a relation with substanceness (*dravyatva*) qualified by inherence in their own substratum;
for, regarding such inherence and substanceness, there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*).
Because, in the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*), there would result a multiplicity of causalities;

for since the relation consisting of both temporal connection (*kālika*) and inherence (*samavāya*) serves as the delimitor of the delimitation of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*), existence (*sattā*), despite being common to eternal entities, [does not entail such a consequence].

The detailed explanation of "deficiency" (kṣati) is found elsewhere [in the text]. Regarding the phrase "by itself alone" (svata eva): being excluded by itself (svato vyāvṛttatva) means not being the object of an inference that—having a mark (liṅga) distinct from itself and having itself as its qualificandum (viśeṣya)—establishes its difference from others of its own class.

And "belonging to the same class" (sājātya) is understood in the form of a property that serves as a differentiator of categories (padārthavibhājakopādhi). Therefore, there is no defect even if a jar (*ghaṭa*) and the like are excluded [from the category of substance] by way of identity (*tādātmya*), nor even if a particular (*viśeṣa*) is the object of an inference of difference from others due to its being devoid of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, nor even if substances (*dravya*) and the like are similar to particulars by virtue of being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and so forth.

The statement that "they reside in eternal substances" is a description of the locus of *viśeṣas*, not part of their definition, as it serves no purpose there. Regarding their exclusion from other things: if it is argued that "atomicity (*paramāṇutva*) and so forth will serve as the differentiators, so what is the need for *viśeṣas*?", we say no; for a property that is itself not excluded [from others] cannot function as a differentiator.
Because it is impossible for [a particular] to be a differentiator, there would be an infinite regress if one required another differentiator for it.

If it is argued that this undesirable consequence applies to the particulars (*viśeṣas*) themselves, we say no; for they are established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends their substratum as being differentiated by their own nature. And thus, the particulars exist in eternal substances.
The perfected ones (siddhas) [are described] in the Dinakarī:
"But their qualities do not possess further particulars (*viśeṣa*), for they are distinguished solely by their substratum."
The point is that because the substratum is excluded [from others] and possesses specific qualities, it is possible for it to be a *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity).

Others also say that since exclusion from God and space is possible through eternal cognition and sound respectively, there is no need for a *viśeṣa* in those cases. However, the moderns [hold a different view].

They say that there is no evidence for a distinct entity called *viśeṣa* (particularity); for by the very same [reason] through which the particulars possess distinctness even without the property of self-manifestation (*svavṛttidharma*), eternal substances likewise possess it. [The relation is as follows: The relation of jars and the like is with their constituent potsherds;
that of substances is with qualities and actions; and that of these [qualities and actions] is with their universals (*jāti*). This is the relation.

The root [text] states: "In that regard, the words 'jar' and 'potsherd' refer to the whole and its parts," as expressed in the phrase "of the part and the whole. And by the word "jāti" (genus), as noted in the *Dinakarī*, the conjunction "ca" (and) includes the relation of *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity) in eternal substances.
Thus he says: "Of eternal substances and particulars.
He states the definition of inherence (samavāya): "The state of being an eternal relation. Furthermore, the relation must be understood as distinct from its relata;
therefore, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to the essential nature of eternal absences and the like, which are relations by their very nature. Now, [an objection]:...
Anticipating the objection, "What is the proof for the relationhood of inherence (*samavāya*)?", he says: "The proof for that, however...

By the phrase "qualities, actions, etc.," the inclusion of universals (*jāti*) is intended. Regarding "conjunction (*saṃyoga*), etc.": the sense is that there is a restrictive rule that conjunction occurs only between two substances. Here, by way of the relation of inherence...

Since thread-ness (*tantutva*) is the cause of cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) as delimited by it through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), the inherence relation (*samavāya*) is established as the mode of the delimiting relation of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka-sambandha*). Nor should it be argued that one should instead postulate a causal relation by substituting the "essential relation" (*svarūpa-sambandha*) for inherence; for if that were the case, [the following would occur]:
"That in which the effect inheres when it is produced is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)"—

if this were not accepted, the determination of the inherent cause would be impossible. Nor should it be argued that "that which is connected with the effect when it is produced is the inherent cause," because [this definition would over-extend] to the destruction of a jar, which is connected to the potsherds.
It should also be observed that [this leads to] the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the skull would be the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*): this is to be understood as referring to the opponent who asserts that the relation between two inseparable entities (*ayutasiddha*) is one of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*). Regarding the phrase "or a different matter" (*arthāntara*): this refers to those engaged in proving inherence (*samavāya*).

The phrase "of the Naiyāyikas" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Or "another object" (arthāntaram): the phrase "of the Naiyāyikas who are engaged in proving inherence" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Now, even so, what is the proof for the oneness of inherence? To this he says: "due to parsimony" (lāghavāt). And thus, just as...
The meaning is that, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), God is established as being one alone by virtue of being the generator of earth and so forth;

likewise, so too is inherence (*samavāya*). "By a cognition possessing color" means that there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a cognition possessing color would be a valid cognition (*pramā*).

The sense is that there is identity between the inherence of touch and the inherence of color. Regarding the phrase "in that [air]," it means because of the absence of color. Now, one might object: if the inherence of color exists there, how can there be an absence of color in that [air] through that very relation? For where a relation exists, [the related thing must also exist] through that relation. (Dinakari)
It should be stated that [the relation] is not pervaded by the existence of related substances,

because only an inherence qualified by being determined by color (*rūpa*) constitutes the relation of color, and such a relation is absent in air. Nor can it be argued that, since the qualified is not distinct from its constituents, the qualified inherence is also [absent].

It must be stated that [the relation] does not exist in air; for the relation of color consists precisely in the substratum-ness (adhikaraṇatā) as determined by inherence (samavāya) which is itself qualified by being determined by color, and that [inherence] is absent in air. [Likewise], the inherence of odor in earth [is not the relation of odor].
The moderns, however, hold that inherence (*samavāya*) is manifold based on such cognitions as "in water" and so forth;

the ellipsis for "another relation" is "as a distinct category. The phrase "it would be established" implies "on the ground" and so forth. If a distinct entity called "qualificative relation" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is accepted, then...

Regarding the dilemma as to whether that [absence] is eternal or non-eternal, he states the refutation of the first position with the words "of that" (*tasya*). Now, one might object: even if the absence of the jar exists there [in the location], at the time when the jar is being brought in, the cognition of the absence of the jar does not arise simply because the absence of the absence of the jar is present; therefore, he says "of the absence of the jar. In that case...

"On the ground possessing a jar" (*ghaṭavati bhūtale*). "Of that" (*tasyeti*) means "of the absence of the jar" (*ghaṭābhāvasya*). Otherwise, [if it were not so], if the absence of the jar were non-eternal (*anityatve*), then even in another location—that is, even in a place devoid of a jar—the same would follow.
The point is that the absence delimited by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna-abhāva*) is of a single nature. Regarding "of the specific relation" (*vaiśiṣṭya-syeti*).

This refers to the position that accepts the eternality of *vaiśiṣṭya* (the relation of inherence) and so forth. In that context, regarding a locus possessing a jar through the bringing of a jar: one should not say that there is no cognition of the absence of a jar in a locus possessing a jar because the cognition of the possession of a jar—which acts as an obstacle—is present; for [this rule applies] to the case where a cognition arises during a state in which the cognition of the possession of a jar is absent. (Dinakarī)

This is because the intended meaning [of the original argument] is that it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the cognition of the absence of a jar would be a valid cognition (*pramā*). Now, one might object:

"Even according to the view of the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), since the inherence (*samavāya*) of the dark color exists in a jar that has been turned red by baking, there would be the consequence of a cognition [of that jar] as possessing the dark color. To this, he says: "But for me... [and so on]. In the second case...

He states the refutation: "of the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*). Now, if one asks, "If the relation of qualification is not admitted, what is the relation between the absence of a jar and the ground? Is it their own nature (*svarūpa*)?"—if that were the case, then even when the ground possesses a jar, [the cognition of the absence] would occur just as it does in the state when the ground is devoid of a jar.

"In your view as well, the cognition of the absence of a jar would occur, because the absence of the jar, the ground, and their relation of essential identity (svarūpa-sambandha) are present there; therefore, he says: 'If this were so' (*evaṃ ceti*). 'Belonging to that particular time' (*tattatkālīnam*) means belonging to the time of the cognition 'the ground is devoid of a jar'."

"Such and such a ground and so forth" means that where there is the cognition of the absence of a jar on a particular ground, it is that specific ground and so forth. "Of such and such absences" means of whichever particular absence there is a cognition, it is of that very one. And thus, it is not the mere intrinsic nature [of the locus] alone.
The meaning is that the relation is not like this, but rather a specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*), as stated by Dinakara;

thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) mentioned previously. However, the moderns (*navya*) maintain that "distinctness" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is indeed a separate category (*padārthāntara*), because of the cognition: "the ground possesses the absence of a jar."

And they say that if one accepts an essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), there is a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) because one could instead take as the basis for the absence the cognition whose object is merely the undivided difference residing in the locus of the absence, and so forth. [End of section 1. Regarding the phrase "the mutual absence among the six categories beginning with substance":

In this context, it should be noted that *dravyatva* (substancehood) and the like are not the delimiters of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) because they lack uniformity; rather, it is the specific property such as "cloth-ness" residing in them—just as "duality" is the delimiter for a difference having two things as its counter-correlates.
In reality, however, being distinct from absence (*bhāvabhinnatva*) itself should be understood as such. On this point, some say:

If the nature of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāvatva*) were itself non-existence (*abhāvatva*), then at a time when one lacks the cognition of its defining attribute— namely, "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*)— the cognition "the jar does not exist" would not arise.
This same [argument applies] later to the nature of mutual absence, which contains within it the element of non-existence.
If the nature of being an absence (*abhāvatva*) were to contain within it the nature of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāvatva*), there would arise the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Likewise, if the nature of being an absence were defined as being different from existence (*bhāva*),

then the verbal cognition arising from the sentence "absence is not existence" would be impossible, because the delimiting factor of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) would be identical.

Therefore, they say that "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) is either a specific kind of relatum (*anuyogitā-viśeṣa*) or an indivisible over-extension (*akhaṇḍopādhi*). Regarding this, the moderns (*navya*) state: there is no evidence for absence-ness being an indivisible over-extension; rather, it is simply the state of being different from an entity (*bhāva-bhinnatva*).

That [absence] consists in the absence of existence (sattā) whose counter-positiveness is delimited by either the relation of inherence (samavāya) or the relation of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya); and although this has not been previously presented [to consciousness], it serves as the qualifier (prakāra). In this way, the commonality among the cognitions of the absence of a jar and the absence of a cloth is established with respect to the aspect of their being absences. Nor is there...

There is no infinite regress regarding the objective status (*viṣayatā*), because it is admitted that the manifestation of the absolute non-existence of "being" (*sat*) is itself a qualifier by its very nature. For this very reason, even without the cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) in the form of "being," that [non-existence] is the qualifier in the cognition "the jar does not exist"; it is indeed a perception qualified by the property of being an absence (*abhāvatva*).

This is because the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogidhī*) is the cause [of the cognition of absence]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition "this is darkness" could not arise. Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the cause being the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇadhī*), given that the property of being an absence (*abhāvatva*), which consists in the absence of existence, is not present as a qualifier.

They say that because the nature of being a cause differs according to the difference in qualifiers, the status of being a cause for that [result] is not admitted there; for conceptual construction conforms to the result.

From the root text, "due to the distinction between relational non-existence (saṃsargānyonyābhāva) and mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva)," it might be understood that one is called "relational" and the other "mutual. However, that is incorrect, because it is not accepted that a relation itself is a type of non-existence. Therefore, he says: "relational non-existence... Thus, the word "non-existence" (abhāva), which is heard at the end of the dvandva compound...

The intended meaning of the root text is that, because each [term] is related [to non-existence], there are both "relational non-existence" (*saṃsargābhāva*) and "mutual non-existence" (*anyonyābhāva*).
He states the definitions of these two non-existences in sequence: "the state of being relational non-existence" (*saṃsargābhāvatvam*), and so forth.
The phrase "distinct from mutual non-existence" (*anyonyābhāvabhinna*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) into the case of mutual non-existence. (Dinakari)
The term "absence" (*abhāva*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to objects such as jars; the same applies in the subsequent cases. Regarding the phrase "identity" (*tādātmya*):

what is intended by the term "identity" is that the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by identity (*tādātmya*) as its delimitor. By this, [the definition does not apply] to the absolute absence of a conjoined object (*saṃyogin*), whose counter-positiveness is delimited by conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

There is no over-extension [of the definition]. He states the definition of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as "being a non-existence that is destructible. Here, the term "destructible" (*vināśī*) is used to exclude over-extension to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). If it is asked, "What is the proof for the existence of antecedent non-existence?", the ancients maintain that its establishment follows from the fear that what has already arisen might arise again.

Some, however, hold that destruction is distinct from non-existence due to the force of perception, as in the case of "the jar has been produced" (*jāto ghaṭaḥ*) versus "the destruction of the jar has arisen" (*utpanno ghaṭadhvaṃsaḥ*). They argue that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not [distinct], because people lack the cognition "here now there is the prior non-existence of the jar. And this is not so... [end of fragment].

Since the pot-shards that produce that jar, their conjunction, and so forth, continue to exist even at the time of that jar's production, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of that jar being produced yet again. If one were to accept prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), it must be said that its production occurs only because of the absence of that [prior non-existence]. This is with respect to [the effect] delimited by the property of being a produced substance (janya-dravyatva).

This consequence is impossible because of the absence of the non-existence of substance— which is established as the cause [of destruction]— wherein the counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Nor can it be argued that the cause is either the non-existence of a produced substance,
or the non-existence of a destruction whose origination occurs at the same time as the origination of the produced substance.

Due to the absence of any decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*), and because of the parsimony (*lāghava*) of postulating a single cause rather than the causal status of both such absences of substance and such absences of destruction, [only one is accepted].
